summary: Lays out a framework for running IP over optical networks. It covers both an IP-based control plane for optical networks and how IP and optical layers interact, including routing and signaling. It reflects the industry view that IP-based protocols could control optical equipment. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Fiber cables carry light, and routers carry internet traffic. This note explains how the two can talk and cooperate so the light paths get set up by the same kinds of rules.

questions: how do routers control optical networks
subtitle: Merging routers and fiber optics with a common control system

tldr.problem: High-speed routers and optical networks are becoming integrated, but they need a common way to set up and manage the fiber paths that carry traffic between routers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a framework where IP-based control protocols manage optical networks the same way routers manage packet forwarding, using standards like GMPLS for signaling and routing.
tldr.outcome: This framework enables dynamic provisioning of lightpaths (optical circuits), automatic restoration when links fail, and support for both integrated and overlay architectures depending on operational needs.

facts.label: Wavelengths per fiber
facts.value: Can exceed 160 in dense WDM systems

today: RFC 3717 is Informational, describing a framework rather than a standard. It has not been obsoleted. The mechanisms it discusses—GMPLS control of optical networks, peer and overlay interconnection models, and lightpath provisioning—remain foundational to modern photonic network control architecture, though the specific standards have evolved through related RFCs like RFC 3471 and RFC 3473.

sections.title: The Problem of IP and Optical Integration
sections.content:
Internet traffic infrastructure is moving toward high-speed routers at the network edge connected by optical core networks. However, the two systems spoke different languages: routers used IP-based protocols, while optical networks used different control mechanisms. The RFC addresses a fundamental architectural question: how should IP networks and optical networks coordinate to share control of the fiber paths that connect them?

The framework recognizes that optical networks must be survivable (recover from failures), flexible (adapt to changing traffic), and controllable (allow intelligent routing). At the same time, there is a push in the industry to adopt IP-based protocols for the optical control plane, rather than inventing optical-specific protocols. This means reusing routing and signaling mechanisms developed for IP traffic engineering.
sections.eli5: Routers and optical networks need to work together, but they don't naturally speak the same language. The solution is to teach both systems to use the same IP-based language for controlling the fiber paths.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Building Blocks
sections.content:
The framework introduces several essential terms. A lightpath is an optical circuit connecting two points end-to-end through the optical network. The optical cross-connect (OXC) is a switching device that routes optical signals from input ports to output ports. Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM) allows multiple signals at different wavelengths to travel on one fiber simultaneously.

Two network types are described: opaque networks convert optical signals to electricity at each switch (adding 3R regeneration: re-power, retiming, reshaping), while transparent networks keep signals in the optical domain. The framework also defines interfaces: the User-Network Interface (UNI) between clients and the optical network, and the Network-to-Network Interface (NNI) between optical switches.
sections.eli5: Think of lightpaths as reserved lanes on the optical highway, cross-connects as highway interchanges, and wavelengths as different colored light rays all traveling on the same fiber. UNI is where you enter the optical system; NNI is how the system's internal switches talk to each other.

sections.title: Architectural Models for IP-Optical Interaction
sections.content:
The RFC presents three main architectural approaches. The peer model treats IP routers and optical switches as equals, running the same instance of a control protocol across both domains. This works well within a single administrative domain where both systems are under unified management.

The overlay model keeps the IP and optical control planes completely separate, like classical IP over ATM. The optical network may use its own routing and signaling protocols independent of what the IP network does. Lightpaths are provisioned on demand or manually configured without deep integration.

The augmented model runs separate routing in each domain but allows some information to flow between them—for example, IP routers learn which optical egress ports lead to external destinations. This middle ground works well across administrative boundaries where domains don't fully trust each other.
sections.eli5: The peer model is like two departments sharing one office manager. The overlay model is like two separate companies in the same building with their own managers. The augmented model is like two departments that share a receptionist but keep separate managers.

sections.title: Routing and Signaling for Lightpath Setup
sections.content:
Routing determines which path through the optical network a lightpath should take. The framework supports several approaches: in integrated routing, a single routing protocol (like OSPF with optical extensions) runs across both IP and optical domains, allowing end-to-end path computation.

Domain-specific routing keeps routing separate in each domain and may use BGP to advertise reachability between them. Overlay routing uses a registry where edge routers register their IP addresses, and other routers query it to find egress points.

For signaling (actually setting up the lightpath), the framework proposes adapting MPLS signaling protocols like RSVP-TE or CR-LDP for lightpath requests. The domain services model offers a simple service interface: create/delete/query lightpaths, with minimal signaling requirements. The unified services model integrates IP and optical signaling so that creating an IP label-switched path automatically creates any necessary lightpaths underneath.
sections.eli5: Routing is like deciding which highway to take. Signaling is like calling the highway authority and saying 'reserve this lane for me now.' Different models handle these decisions differently, from completely separate to tightly integrated.

sections.title: Recovery and Resilience
sections.content:
When a fiber link fails, the optical network must recover the affected lightpaths. The RFC discusses two protection strategies. Segment-wise protection divides an end-to-end path into segments (IP part, optical part, IP part) and protects each segment separately, potentially using protection services at both layers to achieve end-to-end resilience.

Single-layer protection means the IP layer provides all protection without relying on optical network protection. Within a domain, local restoration can quickly reroute around a failed link, while end-to-end restoration reroutes the entire affected lightpath. The framework supports both 1+1 protection (always-on backup) and shared protection (backup paths shared among multiple protected flows, assuming only one failure at a time).

To enable protection, the system must know which links share risk groups (SRLGs)—physical resources that fail together, like fibers in the same conduit. Backup paths must avoid links with the same SRLGs as the primary path.
sections.eli5: Imagine two routes home: one uses the main highway, one uses back streets. Segment-wise protection means each route is protected separately. Single-layer protection means only one route has a backup. Shared protection means several main routes can share the same backup, but only if they don't both fail at once.

sections.title: Path Forward: From Simple to Complex
sections.content:
The RFC recommends an evolutionary approach: start with simple overlay architectures and overlay interconnection, then gradually move toward tighter integration. Early deployments will likely use domain services (simple lightpath requests) with manual or offline provisioning. The next step adds reachability exchange between domains, allowing lightpaths to be established dynamically as part of end-to-end provisioning.

The final stage achieves the full peer model with sophisticated routing interaction. However, the RFC notes that a common signaling framework (GMPLS) from the start enables incremental progress without complete redesign. This phased approach acknowledges that integrating IP and optical control in production networks presents challenges beyond pure technology—administrative, political, and operational barriers exist, especially in multi-vendor and multi-domain environments.
sections.eli5: Start simple with basic lightpath requests, add intelligence over time to handle reachability, and eventually reach full integration. This lets operators learn and add complexity gradually without breaking what already works.
